claim: Lophosteus superbus is from the Late Silurian period, 422 million years old
source: The ontogenetic trajectory of a marginal jawbone of Lophosteus superbus (Late Silurian, 422 Million years old), the phylogenetically most basal stem osteichthyan, visualized by synchrotron microtomography, reveals a developmental relationship between teeth and dermal odontodes that is not evident from the adult morphology.
evidence: The age and geological period are stated directly in the abstract

claim: Lophosteus superbus is the phylogenetically most basal stem osteichthyan
source: The ontogenetic trajectory of a marginal jawbone of Lophosteus superbus (Late Silurian, 422 Million years old), the phylogenetically most basal stem osteichthyan, visualized by synchrotron microtomography, reveals a developmental relationship between teeth and dermal odontodes that is not evident from the adult morphology.
evidence: The phylogenetic position is stated in the abstract and supported by comparative analysis in the manuscript

claim: The earliest odontodes in Lophosteus are two longitudinal founder ridges formed at the ossification center
source: The earliest odontodes are two longitudinal founder ridges formed at the ossification center.
evidence: This is directly observed from the synchrotron microtomography data and 3D reconstruction

claim: Odontodes added lingually to the founder ridges turn into conical teeth and undergo cyclic replacement
source: Subsequent odontodes that are added lingually to the ridges turn into conical teeth and undergo cyclic replacement, while those added labially achieve a stellate appearance.
evidence: This developmental pattern is observed in the 3D reconstruction and ontogenetic analysis

claim: Odontodes added labially to the founder ridges achieve a stellate appearance
source: Subsequent odontodes that are added lingually to the ridges turn into conical teeth and undergo cyclic replacement, while those added labially achieve a stellate appearance.
evidence: This morphological pattern is observed in the specimen analysis

claim: Stellate odontodes deposited directly on the bony plate are aligned with alternate files of teeth
source: Stellate odontodes deposited directly on the bony plate are aligned with the alternate files of teeth, whereas new tooth positions are inserted into the files of sequential addition when a gap appears.
evidence: This alignment pattern is demonstrated through 3D modeling and analysis

claim: New tooth positions are inserted into files of sequential addition when a gap appears
source: Stellate odontodes deposited directly on the bony plate are aligned with the alternate files of teeth, whereas new tooth positions are inserted into the files of sequential addition when a gap appears.
evidence: This developmental process is observed in the ontogenetic reconstruction

claim: Successive teeth and overgrowing odontodes show hybrid morphologies around the oral-dermal boundary
source: Successive teeth and overgrowing odontodes show hybrid morphologies around the oral-dermal boundary, suggesting signal cross-communication.
evidence: The hybrid morphologies are observed in the specimen and interpreted as evidence of signal interaction

claim: Teeth and dermal odontodes are modifications of a single system, regulated and differentiated by the oral and dermal epithelia
source: We propose that teeth and dermal odontodes are modifications of a single system, regulated and differentiated by the oral and dermal epithelia.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation based on the developmental observations

claim: A tooth is a particular type of odontode
source: A tooth is a particular type of 'odontode' (Figure 1A): an exoskeletal structure that forms at an interface between an epithelial fold and the underlying mesenchyme, by dentine growing inwards from the epithelial contact surface.
evidence: This is a definitional statement based on established knowledge

claim: An odontode forms at an interface between an epithelial fold and the underlying mesenchyme, by dentine growing inwards from the epithelial contact surface
source: A tooth is a particular type of 'odontode' (Figure 1A): an exoskeletal structure that forms at an interface between an epithelial fold and the underlying mesenchyme, by dentine growing inwards from the epithelial contact surface.
evidence: This describes the developmental process based on established knowledge

claim: A mature odontode consists of dentine, in some cases covered with enamel or other hypermineralized surface tissue, irrigated through a central pulp cavity or pulp canals, and attached by a vascularized bone-like tissue
source: A mature odontode consists of dentine, in some cases covered with enamel or other hypermineralized surface tissue, irrigated through a central pulp cavity or pulp canals, and attached by a vascularized bone-like tissue (Ørvig, 1977; Smith and Hall, 1993; Huysseune and Sire, 1998; Karatajute‐Talimaa, 1998).
evidence: This structural description is supported by cited literature

claim: Teeth are the only odontodes to persist in tetrapods
source: Although teeth are the only odontodes to persist in tetrapods (Reif, 1982), various forms of dermal odontodes covered the entire body surface of many extinct jawless vertebrates, before jaws and teeth evolved (Janvier, 1996), and persist in some extant groups.
evidence: This evolutionary pattern is supported by cited literature

claim: Various forms of dermal odontodes covered the entire body surface of many extinct jawless vertebrates before jaws and teeth evolved
source: Although teeth are the only odontodes to persist in tetrapods (Reif, 1982), various forms of dermal odontodes covered the entire body surface of many extinct jawless vertebrates, before jaws and teeth evolved (Janvier, 1996), and persist in some extant groups.
evidence: This is supported by cited paleontological literature

claim: Placoid scales of sharks are commonly called 'skin teeth'
source: Probably, the most familiar examples of dermal odontodes in extant vertebrates are the placoid scales of sharks, which are commonly called 'skin teeth'.
evidence: This is a statement of common terminology

claim: Multiple dermal odontodes can be fused to a basal plate in the growing scales of primitive chondrichthyans
source: Besides this form of individual pointed denticles, multiple dermal odontodes can be fused to a basal plate, like in the growing scales of primitive chondrichthyans (Reif, 1978b), or anchored on a dermal bone, like on the skull bones of primitive osteichthyans, where the odontodes are usually accreted into patterned tubercles or ridges, referred to as 'ornament'.
evidence: This structural arrangement is supported by cited literature

claim: Dermal odontodes on skull bones of primitive osteichthyans are usually accreted into patterned tubercles or ridges, referred to as 'ornament'
source: Besides this form of individual pointed denticles, multiple dermal odontodes can be fused to a basal plate, like in the growing scales of primitive chondrichthyans (Reif, 1978b), or anchored on a dermal bone, like on the skull bones of primitive osteichthyans, where the odontodes are usually accreted into patterned tubercles or ridges, referred to as 'ornament'.
evidence: This describes a morphological pattern in primitive osteichthyans

claim: Dermal odontodes have long been regarded as an independent developmental module distinct from teeth because of their supposed lack of temporo-spatial regulation
source: Dermal odontodes have long been regarded as an independent developmental module distinct from teeth, because of their supposed lack of the temporo-spatial regulation that, in teeth, is provided by a specific epithelial structure such as a dental lamina or odontogenic band (Reif, 1982; Fraser and Smith, 2011).
evidence: This describes a historical scientific perspective supported by citations

claim: Shark placoid scales were recently shown to be patterned by a Turing-like mechanism
source: However, shark placoid scales were recently shown to be patterned by a Turing-like mechanism (Maisey and Denton, 2016; Cooper et al., 2018).
evidence: This recent finding is supported by cited literature

claim: Current knowledge about the growth patterns of dermal odontodes is basically limited to modern sharks
source: Nevertheless, current knowledge about the growth patterns of dermal odontodes is basically limited to modern sharks.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of knowledge in the field

claim: The classic 'outside-in' hypothesis for tooth evolution is currently in favor after decades of debate
source: The classic 'outside-in' hypothesis is currently in favor after decades of debate (Donoghue and Rücklin, 2014; Haridy et al., 2019), but the developmental continuum between teeth and dermal odontodes, which is one of its central premises, still lacks unequivocal evidence.
evidence: This describes the current state of scientific consensus with citations

claim: The developmental continuum between teeth and dermal odontodes still lacks unequivocal evidence
source: The classic 'outside-in' hypothesis is currently in favor after decades of debate (Donoghue and Rücklin, 2014; Haridy et al., 2019), but the developmental continuum between teeth and dermal odontodes, which is one of its central premises, still lacks unequivocal evidence.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge

claim: Extant gnathostomes with dermal odontodes always display a sharp demarcation between teeth and ornament
source: Extant gnathostomes with dermal odontodes (sharks, rays, and some bony fishes such as Polypterus) always display a sharp demarcation between teeth and ornament.
evidence: This is an observational statement about extant taxa

claim: The marginal jawbone specimen GIT 760-12 was scanned with an isotropic voxel size of 0.696 µm
source: A marginal jawbone of Lophosteus, GIT 760–12 (Figure 3A) from the Late Silurian (Pridoli) of Ohessaare Cliff, Saaremaa, Estonia, was scanned with an isotropic voxel (3D pixel) size of 0.696 µm.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the scanning parameters

claim: The specimen GIT 760-12 is probably from the lower jaw as it carries a lateral line groove that parallels the jaw margin
source: This specimen is probably from the lower jaw as it carries a lateral line groove that parallels the jaw margin.
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical features observed in the specimen

claim: The jawbone can be divided into oral and facial laminae, which form a transverse angle of about 130°
source: It can be divided into oral and facial laminae, which form a transverse angle of about 130° (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a measurement from the specimen analysis

claim: The ossification center is located at the boundary of the oral and facial laminae, the thickest point of the bony plate
source: The ossification center is located at the boundary of the two laminae, the thickest point of the bony plate.
evidence: This is determined from anatomical analysis of the specimen

claim: The feeder vessels of the odontode layer all radiate from the ossification center
source: The feeder vessels of the odontode layer, which penetrate the bony plate with an increasing diameter and obliquity from lingual to labial, all radiate from here (Figure 3C, sky blue; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and Figure 5A, arrows).
evidence: This vascular pattern is observed in the 3D reconstruction

claim: A layer of large cuboidal osteocyte lacunae may represent the oldest part of the jawbone that was deposited rapidly during the earliest developmental stage
source: A layer of large cuboidal osteocyte lacunae (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B; Figure 4—figure supplement 2) may represent the oldest part of the jawbone (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, dashed curve) that was deposited rapidly during the earliest developmental stage (Davesne et al., 2020).
evidence: This interpretation is based on histological observations and cited literature

claim: The oldest odontodes in the entire system are two rows of first-generation odontodes fused into longitudinal ridges with confluent pulp cavities at the level of the probable ossification center
source: The oldest odontodes in the entire system are two rows of first-generation odontodes, fused into longitudinal ridges with confluent pulp cavities, at the level of the probable ossification center (Figures 2A, 3C and 4B; Figure 3—figure supplement 2, FRla, FRlin).
evidence: This is observed from the 3D reconstruction and ontogenetic analysis

claim: On the lingual founder ridge, the main cusps are tall, conical, lingually recurved and widely spaced
source: On the lingual founder ridge, the main cusps are tall, conical, lingually recurved and widely spaced; on the labial founder ridge they are blade-like, labially inclined and united by small cusps.
evidence: This morphological description is based on direct observation of the specimen

claim: On the labial founder ridge, the main cusps are blade-like, labially inclined and united by small cusps
source: On the lingual founder ridge, the main cusps are tall, conical, lingually recurved and widely spaced; on the labial founder ridge they are blade-like, labially inclined and united by small cusps.
evidence: This morphological description is based on direct observation of the specimen

claim: The labial flanks of both founder ridges carry more side-cusps than the lingual flanks
source: The labial flanks of both ridges carry more side-cusps than the lingual flanks (Figures 4B and 5F).
evidence: This morphological pattern is observed in the specimen

claim: There is no overlap between the two founder ridges; instead, their bases join as a continuous sheet, implying they formed simultaneously
source: There is no overlap between the two ridges; instead, their bases join as a continuous sheet (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), implying they formed simultaneously.
evidence: This is an observation leading to an inference about timing of formation

claim: Following the establishment of the founder ridges, more isolated odontodes were added sequentially in both lingual and labial directions
source: Following the establishment of the founder ridges, more isolated odontodes were added sequentially in both lingual and labial directions, overlapping the lingual and labial edges of the founder ridges, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, O1g-2–1 and TF5-3).
evidence: This developmental sequence is reconstructed from the specimen

claim: New odontodes on the lingual side of the lingual ridge are unicuspid, conical teeth
source: These new odontodes are unicuspid, conical teeth on the lingual side of the lingual ridge (Figure 5F), but are multicuspid and quickly take on the stellate morphology with crenulated ridges on the labial side of the labial ridge (Figure 4B).
evidence: This morphological pattern is observed in the specimen

claim: New odontodes on the labial side of the labial ridge are multicuspid and quickly take on the stellate morphology with crenulated ridges
source: These new odontodes are unicuspid, conical teeth on the lingual side of the lingual ridge (Figure 5F), but are multicuspid and quickly take on the stellate morphology with crenulated ridges on the labial side of the labial ridge (Figure 4B).
evidence: This morphological pattern is observed in the specimen

claim: As the odontode skeleton spreads away from the two founder ridges, it turns into teeth lingually and into ornament labially
source: Simply put, as the odontode skeleton spreads away from the two founder ridges, it turns into teeth lingually and into ornament labially.
evidence: This is a summary of the observed developmental pattern

claim: In the rows that follow lingually from the lingual founder ridge, all the main cusps become isolated and sharp
source: In the rows that follow lingually from the lingual founder ridge, all the main cusps become isolated and sharp.
evidence: This morphological change is observed in the specimen

claim: The unicuspid odontodes following the lingual founder ridge are arranged in semi-regular alternate files
source: Although variable in size, they are arranged in semi-regular alternate files, and the lingual founder ridge can be regarded as a union of two alternate rows (Figure 4B,C; Figure 5A, TP3-1, TP5-1, TP7-1 and TP4-2, TP6-2).
evidence: This organizational pattern is observed in the 3D reconstruction

claim: Only the most labial first-generation teeth are complete
source: Only the most labial (and thus oldest) first-generation teeth are complete.
evidence: This preservation pattern is observed in the specimen

claim: More lingually, the first-generation teeth are resorbed semi-basally, and their remaining bases overlap considerably
source: More lingually, the first-generation teeth are resorbed semi-basally, and their remaining bases overlap considerably (Figures 2B and 5F), just like the first-generation teeth of the tooth cushions that form the inner dental arcades (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This resorption pattern is observed in the specimen and compared to cited literature

claim: The resorption surfaces of first-generation teeth are wide open to the next first-generation tooth to be added to the file and to the replacement tooth buds that formed immediately above them
source: The resorption surfaces are wide open, not only to the next first-generation tooth to be added to the file, but also to the replacement tooth buds that formed immediately above them (Figure 5C–F).
evidence: This anatomical relationship is observed in the 3D reconstruction

claim: The first-generation teeth establish the tooth positions for the cyclic replacement teeth
source: The first-generation teeth thus establish the tooth positions for the cyclic replacement teeth (Figure 2C,D; Video 1).
evidence: This developmental relationship is inferred from the observed pattern

claim: The pulp cavities of the first-generation teeth lie directly on the basal compact bone, coinciding with the territory of the basal feeder vessels
source: The pulp cavities of the first-generation teeth lie directly on the basal compact bone, coinciding with the territory of the basal feeder vessels (Figure 5A).
evidence: This anatomical relationship is observed in the specimen

claim: The most lingual row of first-generation teeth was once located at the jaw margin and the oral lamina at this early developmental stage was much narrower
source: This indicates that the most lingual row of first-generation teeth was once located at the jaw margin and that the oral lamina at this early developmental stage was much narrower (Figure 2B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1, TF).
evidence: This is an inference about earlier developmental stages based on anatomical observations

claim: Following labially from the labial founder ridge is a single row of isolated spiny odontodes
source: Following labially from the labial founder ridge is a single row of isolated spiny odontodes (Figures 2B, 4B and 5A).
evidence: This morphological pattern is observed in the specimen

claim: The isolated spiny odontodes overlap the labial edge of the labial founder ridge substantially, without partially resorbing it
source: They overlap the labial edge of the labial founder ridge substantially, without partially resorbing it.
evidence: This developmental pattern is observed in the specimen

claim: As the facial lamina extends labially, younger generations of odontodes are initiated to cover the new bone
source: As the facial lamina extends labially, younger generations of odontodes are initiated to cover the new bone; as the jawbone rotates labially, they also begin to invade the oral lamina (Figure 2C,D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1, O2g, O3g; Video 1).
evidence: This developmental process is reconstructed from the specimen

claim: As the jawbone rotates labially, younger generations of odontodes begin to invade the oral lamina
source: As the facial lamina extends labially, younger generations of odontodes are initiated to cover the new bone; as the jawbone rotates labially, they also begin to invade the oral lamina (Figure 2C,D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1, O2g, O3g; Video 1).
evidence: This developmental process is reconstructed from the specimen

claim: Unlike the teeth, no resorption occurs in the dermal odontodes
source: Unlike the teeth, no resorption occurs in the dermal odontodes.
evidence: This is an observation from the specimen analysis

claim: Younger generations of larger odontodes overgrow, rather than replace, the preexisting dermal odontodes
source: Younger generations of larger odontodes thus simply overgrow, rather than replace, the preexisting dermal odontodes.
evidence: This developmental pattern is observed in the specimen

claim: There are two levels of overgrowth and the dermal odontodes are divided into three generations
source: There are two levels of overgrowth and the dermal odontodes are divided into three generations, inferred from their size and distribution.
evidence: This classification is based on analysis of the specimen

claim: All generations of dermal odontodes follow a global morphologic gradation where those further from the biting margin have more side-cusps, ridgelets, and crenulations
source: All generations of dermal odontodes follow a global morphologic gradation. The further they are from the biting margin at the time they are initiated, the more side-cusps, ridgelets, and crenulations are associated with the main cusp, and the more ascending canals are attached to the flattened pulp cavities.
evidence: This morphological gradient is observed across the specimen

claim: The largest and youngest stellate odontodes have the most elaborate appearance and the most osteodentine-like tissue
source: The largest and youngest stellate odontodes have the most elaborate appearance (Figure 4A, O3g-3–6, O3g-7) and the most osteodentine-like tissue (Figure 4—figure supplements 2–5), which probably reflects their location furthest from the jaw margin, rather than their size or age.
evidence: This morphological pattern is observed and interpreted in relation to position

claim: The morphological pattern of dermal odontodes reflects a morphogenetic signal gradient between the jaw margin and the generic dermal surface of the face
source: We surmise that this pattern reflects a morphogenetic signal gradient (Figure 4) between the jaw margin and the 'generic dermal surface' of the face, represented here by the facial lamina beyond the lateral line canal.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed morphological gradient

claim: Where the dermal odontodes invade the tooth-bearing oral lamina, a subtle but important morphologic variability affects the labial surface of some shedding teeth
source: Where the dermal odontodes invade the tooth-bearing oral lamina, a subtle but important morphologic variability affects the labial surface of some shedding teeth.
evidence: This morphological variation is observed in the specimen

claim: Replacement teeth at the marginal positions always have a smooth labial surface
source: The replacement teeth at the marginal positions, like the first-generation teeth, always have a smooth labial surface, but teeth close to the invading ornament often carry side-cusps on the labial face (Figure 4A, arrowhead; Figure 6C,D, TR1-9(2), TR3-7, TR3-10, TR6-9, TR7-3, TR7-7).
evidence: This morphological pattern is observed in the specimen

claim: Teeth close to the invading ornament often carry side-cusps on the labial face
source: The replacement teeth at the marginal positions, like the first-generation teeth, always have a smooth labial surface, but teeth close to the invading ornament often carry side-cusps on the labial face (Figure 4A, arrowhead; Figure 6C,D, TR1-9(2), TR3-7, TR3-10, TR6-9, TR7-3, TR7-7).
evidence: This morphological pattern is observed in the specimen

claim: The dentine of the side-cusps on teeth near invading ornament tends to include some cell spaces
source: The dentine of the side-cusps tends to include some cell spaces.
evidence: This histological feature is observed in the specimen

claim: Teeth near invading ornament show ornament-like characteristics
source: In other words, these teeth show ornament-like characteristics; there appears to be a degree of 'morphologic cross-contamination' between the two odontode sets (Figure 4A, bars in lavender and mint).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed morphological variation

claim: At the invasive front line, both overgrowing odontodes and replacement teeth have a half-tooth half-ornament morphology
source: At the invasive front line, both overgrowing odontodes and replacement teeth have a half-tooth half-ornament morphology (Figure 6C, compare O2g-1 and O2g-2 with TR7-3 and TR7-7), though the replacement teeth are recognizable by their possession of basal resorption surfaces.
evidence: This hybrid morphology is observed in the specimen

claim: The marginal dentitions of Andreolepis and Kosoraspis show a similar combination of transverse alternate tooth files with lingual tooth addition, carried on marginal bones that also bear dermal odontodes on their facial laminae
source: The marginal dentitions of the stem osteichthyan Andreolepis (Late Silurian, Gotland, Sweden) and the 'acanthothoracid' stem gnathostome Kosoraspis (Early Devonian, Prague Basin, Czech Republic) are of particular interest as comparators for Lophosteus because they show a similar combination of transverse alternate tooth files with lingual tooth addition, carried on marginal bones that also bear dermal odontodes on their facial laminae (Chen et al., 2016; Vaškaninová et al., 2020).
evidence: This comparative observation is supported by cited literature

claim: Lophosteus aligns with Andreolepis and differs from stem gnathostomes in showing resorptive tooth shedding
source: Lophosteus aligns with Andreolepis and differs from stem gnathostomes in showing resorptive tooth shedding, a unique osteichthyan characteristic (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This phylogenetic character distribution is supported by cited literature

claim: Resorptive tooth shedding is a unique osteichthyan characteristic
source: Lophosteus aligns with Andreolepis and differs from stem gnathostomes in showing resorptive tooth shedding, a unique osteichthyan characteristic (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This phylogenetic character is supported by cited literature

claim: Some tooth positions in Lophosteus show as many as twenty replacement cycles
source: Indeed, this process is of fundamental importance in shaping the dentition of Lophosteus, with some tooth positions showing as many as twenty replacement cycles.
evidence: This is counted from the specimen analysis

claim: Kosoraspis has a much simpler ontogenetic history without resorption-replacement cycles, essentially corresponding to the first-generation odontodes of Andreolepis
source: Kosoraspis has a much simpler ontogenetic history without resorption-replacement cycles, essentially corresponding to the first-generation odontodes of Andreolepis.
evidence: This is a comparative observation based on the literature

claim: Kosoraspis shows a unidirectional change from small dermal odontodes at the external margin of the jawbone, through gradually larger and progressively more tooth-like dermal odontodes, to teeth
source: Kosoraspis shows a unidirectional change from small dermal odontodes at the external margin of the jawbone, through gradually larger and progressively more tooth-like dermal odontodes, to teeth (Vaškaninová et al., 2020).
evidence: This morphological gradient is described in cited literature

claim: In Kosoraspis, the ossification center is located at the external margin
source: This indicates the ossification center is located at the external margin.
evidence: This is inferred from the morphological gradient in Kosoraspis

claim: The gradient between teeth and dermal odontodes of the first generation appears to be unidirectional in Andreolepis too
source: The gradient between teeth and dermal odontodes of the first generation appears to be unidirectional in Andreolepis too, from a morphology with elongate bases to a more prominently tooth-like morphology with round bases as they approach the jaw margin (Chen et al., 2016, Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This morphological gradient is described in cited literature

claim: The location of the odontode founder region and the bone ossification center is considerably external to the original oral-dermal boundary in Andreolepis
source: Nevertheless, it is certain that the location of the odontode founder region and the bone ossification center is considerably external to the original oral-dermal boundary in Andreolepis.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative analysis

claim: In Lophosteus, the three developmental landmarks (odontode founder region, bone ossification center, and oral-dermal boundary) overlap
source: By contrast, the three developmental landmarks overlap in Lophosteus, which thus displays a bidirectional morphologic gradation in the initial odontode skeleton.
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical analysis of Lophosteus

claim: Lophosteus displays a bidirectional morphologic gradation in the initial odontode skeleton
source: By contrast, the three developmental landmarks overlap in Lophosteus, which thus displays a bidirectional morphologic gradation in the initial odontode skeleton.
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical analysis

claim: The dermal odontodes and teeth of Lophosteus are initiated simultaneously in the form of two parallel and closely spaced founder ridges
source: The dermal odontodes and teeth of Lophosteus are initiated simultaneously in the form of two parallel and closely spaced founder ridges (Figures 2A,B and 4B).
evidence: This developmental pattern is observed in the specimen

claim: The geometric layout of the founder ridges strongly suggests that the initiation site for odontode formation is the boundary between two patterning domains
source: This geometric layout strongly suggests that the initiation site for odontode formation is the boundary between two patterning domains: a labial domain where the odontodes become ornament and a lingual domain where they become teeth.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed geometric pattern

claim: The two patterning domains are covered with two distinct epithelia, referred to as the dermal and oral epithelium
source: Because the development of an odontode is always initiated by an epithelium, we infer that the two domains are covered with two distinct epithelia, which we refer to respectively as the dermal and oral epithelium.
evidence: This is an inference based on developmental biology principles

claim: The cusps of the two founder ridges are already morphologically distinct
source: The cusps of the two founder ridges are already morphologically distinct, and the odontodes that are subsequently produced at their labial and lingual sides quickly acquire the full characteristics of ornament and teeth, respectively.
evidence: This morphological distinction is observed in the specimen

claim: The establishment of complete regulatory cascades for teeth and ornament possibly relates to the initiation of new odontodes on each side moving away from the boundary between the dermal and oral epithelia
source: This must represent the establishment of their complete regulatory cascades, and possibly relates to the initiation of new odontodes on each side moving away from the boundary between the dermal and oral epithelia into the presumably more homogeneous signaling environment of a single epithelium (Figure 4, 1g).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the developmental mechanism

claim: Already in the second-generation, stellate odontodes have overgrown some of the oldest teeth, in a considerably more lingual position than the original boundary
source: Already in the second-generation, stellate odontodes have overgrown some of the oldest teeth, in a considerably more lingual position than the original boundary.
evidence: This developmental pattern is observed in the specimen

claim: The third generation of odontodes penetrates even further into the territory of teeth
source: The third generation penetrates even further into the territory of teeth (Figure 4, 2g and 3g; Figure 4—figure supplement 1, O2g, O3g).
evidence: This developmental pattern is observed in the specimen

claim: The invasion of teeth by dermal odontodes suggests an irregular expansion of the dermal epithelium into the region previously occupied exclusively by the oral epithelium
source: This suggests an irregular expansion of the dermal epithelium into the region previously occupied exclusively by the oral epithelium.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed invasion pattern

claim: A similar invasion of the tooth field by dermal ornament has been observed in Andreolepis and an unnamed acanthothoracid from the Canadian Arctic
source: A similar invasion of the tooth field by dermal ornament has been observed in Andreolepis (Chen et al., 2016) and an unnamed acanthothoracid from the Canadian Arctic, specimen CPW.9 (Smith et al., 2017; Vaškaninová et al., 2020).
evidence: This comparative observation is supported by cited literature

claim: In Lophosteus, teeth continue to be replaced cyclically until overgrown by ornament, and the dermal odontodes are never shed
source: Essentially, the deposition of odontodes remains characteristic for the two sets – teeth continue to be replaced cyclically until overgrown by ornament, and the dermal odontodes are never shed – but the morphology of each set seems to become influenced by the other.
evidence: This developmental pattern is observed in the specimen

claim: The morphology of teeth and dermal odontodes seems to become influenced by each other in the invasion zone
source: Essentially, the deposition of odontodes remains characteristic for the two sets – teeth continue to be replaced cyclically until overgrown by ornament, and the dermal odontodes are never shed – but the morphology of each set seems to become influenced by the other.
evidence: This morphological influence is inferred from observations

claim: The teeth nearest to the ornament bear side-cusps that tend to form a labial ridgelet
source: The teeth nearest to the ornament bear side-cusps that tend to form a labial ridgelet.
evidence: This morphological feature is observed in the specimen

claim: In the most lingual dermal odontodes, the conical main cusp tends to stand out and point lingually, the side-cusps being restricted to the labial side
source: Conversely, in the most lingual dermal odontodes, the conical main cusp tends to stand out and point lingually, the side-cusps being restricted to the labial side (Figures 4A,B and 6C,D).
evidence: This morphological feature is observed in the specimen

claim: In the invasion zone, the teeth are ornament-like and the dermal odontodes are tooth-like
source: That is to say, in the invasion zone, the teeth are ornament-like and the dermal odontodes are tooth-like.
evidence: This is a summary of the observed morphological convergence

claim: The simplest explanation for the morphological convergence is that the invasion zone provides a mixed set of morphogenetic signals because it is a patchwork of dermal and oral epithelium
source: The simplest explanation for this phenomenon is that the invasion zone provides a mixed set of morphogenetic signals, because it is a patchwork of dermal and oral epithelium, and that both dermal odontodes and teeth respond to both signals.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanistic explanation

claim: The regulatory cross-contamination only affects the morphology, not the deposition and resorption cycles
source: Note, however, that this 'regulatory cross-contamination' only affects the morphology, not the deposition and (if present) resorption cycles.
evidence: This distinction is observed in the specimen

claim: In Andreolepis, the lingualmost odontodes of any generation of invading ornament can be tall and bear biting damage, in contrast to the characteristic flat-topped ornament morphology
source: In Andreolepis, the lingualmost odontodes of any generation of invading ornament can be tall and bear biting damage, in contrast to the characteristic flat-topped ornament morphology (Chen et al., 2016, Extended Data Figure 3c).
evidence: This comparative observation is from cited literature

claim: In many basal actinopterygians with acrodin-capped teeth, the dermal odontodes labial to the jaw teeth also bear an acrodin cap
source: In many basal actinopterygians with acrodin-capped teeth, such as Birgeria and Boreosomus, the dermal odontodes labial to the jaw teeth also bear an acrodin cap (Ørvig, 1978a, PP. 38, Figs. 3, 4, 7–9).
evidence: This comparative observation is from cited literature

claim: The zone of acrodin-bearing odontodes is invariably restricted to the vicinity of dentition, regardless of the type of jawbone
source: The zone of the acrodin-bearing odontodes varies in size, being, for example, narrower in Colobodus and wider in Nephrotus and others (Ørvig, 1978c, pp. 307), but is invariably restricted to the vicinity of dentition, regardless of the type of jawbone (Ørvig, 1978b, pp. 41–42).
evidence: This pattern is described in cited literature

claim: The labial face of the blade-like teeth on the tooth whorls of Ptomacanthus can be ornamented, like the tesserae that they are interlocked with
source: The labial face of the blade-like teeth on the tooth whorls of Ptomacanthus can be ornamented, like the tesserae that they are interlocked with (Miles, 1973).
evidence: This observation is from cited literature

claim: The toothless Obtusacanthus displays a morphological gradation from stellate head scales, via fan-shaped scales, to tooth-like lip scales
source: The toothless Obtusacanthus displays a morphological gradation from stellate head scales, via fan-shaped scales, to tooth-like lip scales (Blais et al., 2011), comparable to the superficial morphological gradation from stellate facial ornament with crenulated ridgelets, via multicuspid invasive ornament and ornament-like replacement teeth, to unicuspid marginal teeth in Lophosteus.
evidence: This comparative observation is from cited literature

claim: The tooth-like ornament and the ornament-like teeth of Lophosteus call into question the demarcation between dermal and oral developmental domains
source: Together with these observations, the tooth-like ornament and the ornament-like teeth of Lophosteus call into question the demarcation between dermal and oral developmental domains.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the observations

claim: The bone appears to have rotated labially during growth
source: In fact, the bone appears to have rotated labially during growth (Figure 2), so that the location of the mouth margin shifted during ontogeny from the lingual founder ridge, via each lingual row of the first-generation teeth, to each successive row of replacement teeth at the current lingual margin of the oral lamina.
evidence: This developmental process is inferred from the specimen analysis

claim: The oral-dermal epithelial boundary does not drift lingually to any great degree; rather, the rotation of the bone causes the labial tooth rows to move onto the face
source: This implies that the oral-dermal epithelial boundary does not drift lingually to any great degree; rather, the rotation of the bone causes the labial tooth rows to move onto the face, where they get covered by dermal epithelium and overgrown by ornament.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the developmental mechanism

claim: The rotation of the jawbone in Lophosteus is comparable to the rotation of the tooth whorls at the jaw margin of primitive chondrichthyans
source: This is comparable to the rotation of the tooth whorls at the jaw margin of primitive chondrichthyans, with the post-functional teeth slid beneath the skin (Smith and Coates, 2001, Figure 14.3(a); Williams, 2001).
evidence: This comparison is made to cited literature

claim: In Lophosteus, the first-generation teeth are added sequentially toward the growing lingual margin, with the tooth families arranged in horizontal alternate files
source: In Lophosteus, the first-generation teeth are added sequentially toward the growing lingual margin, with the tooth families arranged in horizontal alternate files.
evidence: This developmental pattern is observed in the specimen

claim: Each successor tooth, if not overgrown by invasive odontodes, turns into an initiator and sets up its own tooth family by cyclic replacement
source: In the next stage, each successor, if not overgrown by invasive odontodes, turns into an initiator and sets up its own tooth family by cyclic replacement.
evidence: This developmental process is observed in the specimen

claim: The replacement teeth inherit the pattern of the first-generation teeth, generation after generation, forming vertical alternate columns
source: The replacement teeth hence inherit the pattern of the first-generation teeth, generation after generation, forming vertical alternate columns.
evidence: This organizational pattern is observed in the specimen

claim: The replacement columns, including those inserted later and those disturbed by overgrowing odontodes, follow the same transverse alignment as the first-generation teeth
source: The replacement columns, including those inserted later and those disturbed by overgrowing odontodes, follow the same transverse alignment as the first-generation teeth (Figures 4B, 5 and 6).
evidence: This alignment pattern is observed in the specimen

claim: Sequential addition along the files established by the first generation also applies to the stellate odontodes on the facial lamina
source: Sequential addition along the files established by the first generation also applies to the stellate odontodes on the facial lamina.
evidence: This developmental pattern is observed in the specimen

claim: An alternate arrangement is constant throughout the teeth and tooth-like odontodes on the marginal jawbone of Andreolepis and Kosoraspis
source: Such an alternate arrangement is constant throughout the teeth and tooth-like odontodes on the marginal jawbone of Andreolepis and Kosoraspis as well, irrespective of whether they will be overgrown by younger generations of odontodes (Chen et al., 2016; Vaškaninová et al., 2020).
evidence: This comparative observation is from cited literature

claim: The alternate pattern of teeth and ornament of Lophosteus is already established by the founder ridges
source: The alternate pattern of teeth and ornament of Lophosteus is already established by the founder ridges.
evidence: This developmental pattern is observed in the specimen

claim: The ornament differs from teeth in that every other alternate position of ornament is suppressed as the ornament extends labially
source: The ornament differs from teeth in the fact that every other alternate position of ornament is suppressed as the ornament extends labially (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B); this is because consecutive generations of dermal odontodes increase in length more quickly than the bone.
evidence: This developmental pattern is observed and explained

claim: The replacement of two teeth by a single larger successor at a crowded site has been observed in sharks, frogs and lizards, and considered as a common phenomenon
source: The replacement of two teeth by a single larger successor at a crowded site has been observed in sharks, frogs and lizards, and considered as a common phenomenon (Gillette, 1955; Edmund, 1960; Cooper, 1963; Osborn, 1971; Reif, 1976).
evidence: This comparative observation is from cited literature

claim: In alligator embryos, the reduction of jaw growth can cause the suppression of a tooth family during ontogeny
source: In alligator embryos, the reduction of jaw growth can cause the suppression of a tooth family during ontogeny (Westergaard and Ferguson, 1987).
evidence: This observation is from cited literature

claim: The suppression of tooth positions does not represent an irregularity; instead, it may reflect the fundamental mechanism producing the alternate pattern
source: The suppression does not represent an irregularity; instead, it may reflect the fundamental mechanism producing the alternate pattern.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement about developmental mechanisms

claim: The hexagonal pattern is the most efficient form of close packing of rounded objects
source: The hexagonal pattern is the most efficient form of close packing of rounded objects.
evidence: This is a statement of geometric principle

claim: The close packed teeth of myliobatid rays have turned into short hexagonal prisms
source: The close packed teeth of myliobatid rays, which have turned into short hexagonal prisms (Edmund, 1960; Underwood et al., 2015), is an extreme example of a dentition imitating the structure of a honeycomb.
evidence: This observation is from cited literature

claim: A regular pattern was thought to be unique to teeth and reflect the spatio-temporal regulation of the dental lamina
source: A regular pattern, which was thought to be unique to teeth and reflect the spatio-temporal regulation of the dental lamina (Smith, 2003; Underwood et al., 2016), is actually not uncommon in dermal odontodes, as well as in bony denticles.
evidence: This describes a previous scientific view that is being challenged

claim: Regular patterns are actually not uncommon in dermal odontodes, as well as in bony denticles
source: A regular pattern, which was thought to be unique to teeth and reflect the spatio-temporal regulation of the dental lamina (Smith, 2003; Underwood et al., 2016), is actually not uncommon in dermal odontodes, as well as in bony denticles.
evidence: This is a claim based on comparative observations

claim: Ordered tubercles can be seen covering the armor of jawed stem gnathostomes as long as there is only one generation
source: Ordered tubercles can be seen covering the armor of jawed stem gnathostomes as long as there is only one generation, irrespective of whether they are dentinal units on the gnathal plates and spines, or bony units on the postbranchial lamina (Bystrow, 1957, Fig. 2; Burrow, 2003; Johanson and Smith, 2003; Johanson and Smith, 1999; Young, 2003).
evidence: This observation is from cited literature

claim: In the polyodontode scales of the earliest known chondrichthyans, odontodes are often organized in parallel or radial rows by sequential addition
source: In the polyodontode scales of the earliest known chondrichthyans, odontodes are often organized in parallel or radial rows by sequential addition (Andreev et al., 2020).
evidence: This observation is from cited literature

claim: An alternate pattern can be produced by odontodes that are laid down directly on the bony plate, simply through filling the gaps between the odontodes in the previous row
source: An alternate pattern can be produced by odontodes that are laid down directly on the bony plate, simply through filling the gaps between the odontodes in the previous row, even if the previous row is from the older generation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on observations

claim: It is difficult for the enlarged overgrowing odontodes to find and fit gaps, so the pattern will be disturbed
source: But it is difficult for the enlarged overgrowing odontodes to find and fit such gaps, by reason of the preexisting odontodes, so the pattern will be disturbed.
evidence: This is a logical inference about pattern disruption

claim: In a digitally dissected spine of Romundina, the first generation shows an ordered pattern, but this breaks down in the second and third generations
source: This effect is clearly visible in a digitally dissected spine of the jawed stem gnathostome Romundina, which carries three generations of odontodes (Jerve et al., 2017, Fig. 2D1–D3); the first generation shows an ordered pattern, but this breaks down in the second and third generations.
evidence: This observation is from cited literature

claim: The single-file arrangement of the first-generation odontodes of Andreolepis scale is obscured by the overgrowing odontodes
source: The single-file arrangement of the first-generation odontodes of Andreolepis scale is also obscured by the overgrowing odontodes (Qu et al., 2013).
evidence: This observation is from cited literature

claim: All these examples agree with a fundamental embryologic mechanism of odontode patterning shared among the skeletons of vertebrates, which had evolved prior to the origin of teeth
source: All these examples agree with a fundamental embryologic mechanism of odontode patterning shared among the skeletons of vertebrates, which had evolved prior to the origin of teeth, as already proposed by Osborn, 1971.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion supported by cited literature

claim: The alternate pattern can be self-generating, as long as the size of inhibitory zones is equivalent or in a smooth gradient
source: The alternate pattern can be self-generating, as long as the size of inhibitory zones is equivalent or in a smooth gradient (Osborn, 1977).
evidence: This mechanism is from cited literature

claim: The regularity of organization should not be considered as a criterion of true teeth
source: Therefore, the regularity of organization should not be considered as a criterion of true teeth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative analysis

claim: The claim that the ectoderm (dermal epithelium) lacks patterning capacity is biased by the derived adult condition of modern chondrichthyans
source: The claim that the ectoderm (dermal epithelium) lacks patterning capacity (Fraser and Smith, 2011; Smith and Johanson, 2015), which has been used to support the idea of a fundamental difference between dermal odontodes and teeth, is biased by the derived adult condition of modern chondrichthyans.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of cited literature

claim: Skin denticles of chondrichthyans embryos are added sequentially in regular rows
source: Actually, skin denticles of chondrichthyans embryos are added sequentially in regular rows, including the caudal denticles, dorsal denticles and the first-generation general denticles (Grover, 1974; Reif, 1976; Ballard et al., 1993; Miyake et al., 1999; Johanson et al., 2007; Debiais-Thibaud et al., 2015; Maisey and Denton, 2016; Martin et al., 2016; Cooper et al., 2018).
evidence: This observation is from multiple cited sources

claim: The oro-pharyngeal denticles also emerge in rows in embryos, even if frequently interrupted by the oral papillae and undulated by the uneven surface of the oropharynx
source: The oro-pharyngeal denticles also emerge in rows in embryos, even if frequently interrupted by the oral papillae and undulated by the uneven surface of the oropharynx (Rangel et al., 2017, Fig. 4F,G).
evidence: This observation is from cited literature

claim: All the skin or oral denticles are likely to be self-organized by Turing's reaction-diffusion system, a patterning mechanism probably common to epithelial appendages
source: All the skin or oral denticles are likely to be self-organized by Turing's reaction-diffusion system, a patterning mechanism probably common to epithelial appendages (Maisey and Denton, 2016; Cooper et al., 2018).
evidence: This mechanistic interpretation is from cited literature

claim: Both skin and oropharyngeal denticles retain their alternating pattern in adulthood
source: Even so, both skin and oropharyngeal denticles retain their alternating pattern in adulthood (Rangel et al., 2016).
evidence: This observation is from cited literature

claim: Denticle files with regular spacing line up the rear border of the pharyngeal pads in some requiem sharks, remarkably resembling the tooth files lining the length of jaw
source: Denticle files with regular spacing line up the rear border of the pharyngeal pads in some requiem sharks, remarkably resembling the tooth files lining the length of jaw and probably functioning like osteichthyan pharyngeal dentitions (Nelson, 1970, fig. 13, 15, 16B).
evidence: This observation is from cited literature

claim: Wound-healing experiments on sharks show that the loss of the diagonal rows and the regular size and shape of the scales in repaired squamations is caused by disturbance of the original diagonal arrangement of the anchoring collagen fibers
source: Wound-healing experiments on sharks show that the loss of the diagonal rows and the rostro-caudal polarity as well as the regular size and shape of the scales in repaired squamations is actually caused by disturbance of the original diagonal arrangement of the anchoring collagen fibers (Reif, 1978a).
evidence: This experimental result is from cited literature

claim: The orderly shedding and replacing of chondrichthyan teeth preserves the embryonic pattern
source: By contrast, the orderly shedding and replacing of chondrichthyan teeth preserves the embryonic pattern.
evidence: This is a comparative observation

claim: As a Silurian stem osteichthyan, Lophosteus represents a very short phylogenetic branch in a basal part of the gnathostome crown group
source: Firstly, as a Silurian stem osteichthyan, Lophosteus represents a very short phylogenetic branch in a basal part of the gnathostome crown group, and is thus likely to present primitive characters for the Osteichthyes and maybe for the Gnathostomata as a whole
evidence: This phylogenetic position is based on the analysis in the manuscript

claim: The unified arrangement of the teeth and ornament of Lophosteus challenges the currently popular idea that teeth and dermal denticles have fundamentally different patterning regimes
source: The unified arrangement of the teeth and ornament of Lophosteus challenges the currently popular idea that teeth and dermal denticles have fundamentally different patterning regimes (Fraser and Smith, 2011).
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the observations

claim: In Lophosteus, teeth and ornament are never starkly different
source: In Lophosteus, teeth and ornament are never starkly different.
evidence: This is a summary of the observed morphological continuum

claim: The 'extra-oral teeth' that occur in some teleosts display a regular organization, development in epithelial invaginations, and shedding-replacing by basal resorption
source: Looking further afield, it is noteworthy that the 'extra-oral teeth' that occur in some teleosts also display a regular organization, development in epithelial invaginations, and shedding-replacing by basal resorption of the attachment bone and supporting bone (Sire and Huysseune, 1996; Sire et al., 1998; Sire, 2001; Sire and Allizard, 2001).
evidence: This observation is from cited literature

claim: Extra-oral teeth in teleosts reveal the potential plasticity of odontodes and suggest the conventional criteria of 'true teeth' are in fact not unique to oral teeth
source: These structures reveal the potential plasticity of odontodes and suggest the conventional criteria of 'true teeth' (Burrow, 2003; Smith and Johanson, 2003a; Smith and Johanson, 2003b) are in fact not unique to oral teeth.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on cited literature

claim: Teeth and ornament are homologs
source: Therefore, teeth and ornament are not merely homologs (Reif, 1982; Huysseune and Sire, 1998; Donoghue, 2002), as supported by a common gene regulatory network (Fraser et al., 2010; Debiais-Thibaud et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on homology and gene regulation

claim: Teeth and ornament develop from the same developmental module, modified through a simple mechanism of heterotopy
source: More importantly, they develop from the same developmental module, modified through a simple mechanism of heterotopy (Debiais-Thibaud et al., 2011), which can be evidenced by the developmental continuum, as on the marginal jawbone of Lophosteus.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the observations and cited literature

claim: Teeth did not evolve from ontogenetically mature ornament, but rather from a primordial type of founder odontode, when covered by the oral epithelium
source: However, contrary to the scale-to-teeth scenario of the 'outside-in' theory, we argue that teeth did not evolve from ontogenetically mature ornament, but rather from a primordial type of founder odontode, when covered by the oral epithelium.
evidence: This is a proposed evolutionary scenario based on the observations

claim: The primordial odontodes might be similar all over the body, outside or inside the oropharyngeal cavity, with later deposited odontodes differentiated according to their location and function
source: The primordial odontodes might be similar all over the body, outside or inside the oropharyngeal cavity, with later deposited odontodes differentiated according to their location and function.
evidence: This is a proposed developmental scenario

claim: The primordial odontodes in the ganoid scales of Andreolepis or the cosmoid scales of Psarolepis have a more pointed and tooth-like morphology than the overgrowing odontodes
source: For example, the primordial odontodes in the ganoid scales of Andreolepis or the cosmoid scales of Psarolepis, revealed by PPC-SRµCT, have a more pointed and tooth-like morphology than the overgrowing odontodes (Qu et al., 2013; Qu et al., 2017), resembling the relationship between the founder ridges and ornament in Lophosteus.
evidence: This comparative observation is from cited literature

claim: This earliest developmental stage of the odontode skeleton may have been lost in derived taxa or missed by the conventional investigative techniques
source: This earliest developmental stage of the odontode skeleton may have been lost in derived taxa or missed by the conventional investigative techniques.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for why this pattern hasn't been observed before

claim: Direct comparison between the substantially modified mature subsets of odontodes could lead to the conclusion that teeth and dermal odontodes are two wholly separate systems
source: Direct comparison between the substantially modified mature subsets of odontodes, could lead to the conclusion that teeth and dermal odontodes are two wholly separate systems.
evidence: This is a statement about potential misinterpretation

claim: Only ontogenetic data going back to the earliest stages of development are able to reveal the original patterning relationships within the odontode skeleton
source: Crucially, Lophosteus shows us that only ontogenetic data going back to the earliest stages of development are able to reveal the original patterning relationships within the odontode skeleton.
evidence: This is a methodological conclusion based on the study

claim: The specimen was imaged at beamline ID19 of the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (ESRF) in Grenoble, France
source: The specimen was imaged at beamline ID19 of the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (ESRF) in Grenoble, France, using propagation phase-contrast synchrotron radiation microtomography (PPC-SRµCT) adapted to fossil mineralized tissues histology (Tafforeau and Smith, 2008; Sanchez et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a methodological detail

claim: The scan was obtained with an objective 10×, NA0.3 coupled with a 2× eyepiece
source: With an isotropic voxel size of 0.696 µm, the scan was obtained with an objective 10×, NA0.3 coupled with a 2 × eyepiece.
evidence: This is a methodological detail

claim: The specimen was set up 15 mm from the optics
source: The specimen was set up 15 mm from the optics.
evidence: This is a methodological detail

claim: A total of 4998 projections of 0.3 s each were taken over 360°
source: A total of 4998 projections of 0.3 s each were taken over 360° by half-acquisition of 600 pixels.
evidence: This is a methodological detail

claim: Reconstruction was done with a modified version of a single-distance phase retrieval approach
source: Reconstruction was done with a modified version of a single-distance phase retrieval approach (Paganin et al., 2002; Sanchez et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a methodological detail with citations

claim: The virtual thin sections of the sample were segmented into three-dimensional sub-volumes through the software VG Studio 3.1
source: The virtual thin sections of the sample in the form of stacks of images were segmented into three- dimensional sub-volumes through the software VG Studio 3.1.
evidence: This is a methodological detail

claim: Embedded subtle structures, such as the surfaces of resorption and dentine, were traced manually
source: Embedded subtle structures, such as the surfaces of resorption and dentine, were traced manually.
evidence: This is a methodological detail

claim: Lophosteus completely lacks enamel
source: Lophosteus further resembles a stem gnathostome in completely lacking enamel, whereas Andreolepis has enamel on its scales (Qu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an observed characteristic with comparison to cited literature

claim: Andreolepis has enamel on its scales
source: Lophosteus further resembles a stem gnathostome in completely lacking enamel, whereas Andreolepis has enamel on its scales (Qu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is from cited literature

claim: The only dental character of Lophosteus that unambiguously distinguishes it from acanthothoracids and identifies it as an osteichthyan is the presence of tooth shedding by partial and basal resorption
source: In fact, the only dental character of Lophosteus that unambiguously distinguishes it from acanthothoracids and identifies it as an osteichthyan is the presence of tooth shedding by partial and basal resorption (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This phylogenetic character is supported by cited literature

claim: This character distribution suggests that Lophosteus is the least crownward of known stem osteichthyans
source: This character distribution suggests that Lophosteus is the least crownward of known stem osteichthyans (Figure 1B), making it uniquely informative about the evolution of the osteichthyan dentition.
evidence: This phylogenetic position is inferred from character analysis
